comparison: Both strongly support the system architecture and technical design claims (C1, C2, C11-C15, C60-C75). OpenEval emphasizes technical documentation and replicability, while peer reviewers praise the 'innovative approaches,' 'decentralized Android-based display,' and 'modular architecture.' High agreement on system functionality and design quality.

Both support cost-effectiveness claims (C5, C6, C51, C52). OpenEval notes reasonable cost estimates but mentions lack of specific citations for proprietary system costs (C51). Peer reviewers explicitly recognize cost-effectiveness as a 'major advantage' and 'invaluable resource for budget-friendly' setup. Strong agreement on affordability claims.

Both support position tracking accuracy claims (C18, C19). OpenEval provides detailed validation of methodology using OpenCV ground truth (C85) and acknowledges limitations with lap-reset solution (C83-C84). Peer reviewers accept benchmarking without critique. OpenEval addresses broader validation scope including limitations.

Both support latency benchmarking claims (C24, C25, C26). OpenEval validates methodology and contextualization with mouse reaction times. Peer reviewers affirm 'compelling evidence of functionality' for real-time performance. Complete agreement on system latency validation.

Both support VR architecture claims (C20, C21, C95-C104). OpenEval emphasizes distributed rendering approach and technical soundness. Peer reviewers praise Unity implementation and customizability through behaviorMate/VRMate software. Strong agreement on VR system design and capabilities.

Both support experimental methodology claims (C28-C32). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of sample size, sex balance, surgical procedures, and IACUC approval (C125-C140). Peer reviewers accept methods without critique and acknowledge extensive validation through published studies. Agreement on methodological rigor.

Overlapping support for experimental methods. OpenEval R6 addresses surgical and training protocols (C125-C140), while peer R10 addresses analysis methods (C122-C165). Both accept the methodological approaches as standard and appropriate, with peer reviewers noting adequate documentation.

Both support calcium imaging analysis methods (C122-C157). OpenEval validates Suite2p/OASIS tools, place cell classification criteria, and statistical controls. Peer reviewers accept analysis approaches without concerns. Complete agreement on analysis pipeline appropriateness.

Both support place cell proportion findings (C35, C36). OpenEval notes statistically significant difference but emphasizes complete spatial coverage in both systems as key validation. Peer reviewers affirm 'reliable hippocampal place cell coding' demonstration. Agreement on functional validation despite quantitative differences.

Both support calcium transient property analyses (C37, C38, C42). OpenEval notes appropriate statistics but modest sample size limiting power. Peer reviewers accept findings as part of 'concrete comparison between place cell properties' without raising power concerns. Agreement on results with OpenEval providing more critical statistical assessment.

Both support environment effect findings (C39, C40, C41). OpenEval validates statistical significance and interprets reduced trial-by-trial reliability in VR. Peer reviewers accept as demonstration of 'reliable hippocampal place cell coding.' Complete agreement on these comparative findings.

Both support contextualization with prior literature (C43, C44). OpenEval validates citations and notes cue salience interpretation is speculative but reasonable. Peer reviewers accept findings as 'valuable contribution' comparing treadmill vs. VR navigation. Agreement on interpretation and literature integration.

Both support remapping observations (C45-C49). OpenEval validates Bayesian decoding methodology (C158-C165), cross-validation, and subsampling controls, though notes chance level calculation could be better justified. Peer reviewers accept remapping as supporting system validity without methodological critique. Agreement with OpenEval providing more detailed validation assessment.

Both support system utility claims through published literature (C3, C4, C27, C76-C77, C86-C90, C118-C121). OpenEval notes extensive citations spanning 2016-2023 but clarifies these represent prior work. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'many published studies' and validation through 'myriad experimental paradigms.' Complete agreement on established utility.

Both support background and context claims (C8-C10, C54-C59, C91-C94). OpenEval validates citations as appropriate but notes these represent prior work rather than new contributions. Peer reviewers accept as established context without question. Complete agreement on background literature.

Both support treadmill design features (C78-C82). OpenEval validates functional justifications but notes some claims could benefit from quantitative validation. Peer reviewers accept design and specifically praise 'computer vision-based calibration' as innovative. Agreement with OpenEval noting validation gaps.

Partial overlap on hardware design. OpenEval R15 addresses treadmill features (C105-C107, C112-C117), peer R8 addresses VR implementation and configurations. Both support design flexibility and innovation without critique of specific hardware choices.

Both support system flexibility claims (C97, C98, C108-C111). OpenEval validates tablet-based configuration specifications but notes hybrid setups not demonstrated in validation. Peer reviewers affirm flexibility through Unity implementation and customizability. Agreement on capability claims with OpenEval noting implementation limitations.

Both support open-source accessibility claim (C53). OpenEval notes this distinguishes the system from proprietary alternatives. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'Plug & Play feature requiring no coding experience' as advantage. Agreement on accessibility positioning.

Partial overlap on validation methodology. OpenEval R3 addresses position tracking validation including limitations and lap-reset solution (C83-C85). Peer R7 accepts treadmill design including computer vision calibration. Both support validation approaches without fundamental concerns.

Partial overlap on analysis methods. OpenEval R12 specifically validates Bayesian decoding methodology for remapping (C158-C165). Peer R10 broadly accepts all analysis methods including decoding without specific critique. Agreement on analytical soundness.
